4. Answers cite their sources, and a question with no answer in the docs gets 'I don't know'.
5. The right source is in the top 5 for at least [18 of 20] test questions.
acceptance_checks: A question using different words from the document still finds it.
User B's question never retrieves user A's chunks.
Deleting a document removes it from results and answers.
Answers cite their sources, and a question with no answer in the docs gets 'I don't know'.
The right source is in the top 5 for at least [18 of 20] test questions.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Answers made up from nowhere, results from other users' documents, and stale answers from deleted files.

entries.name: Keeping a search index in sync
needs: search results show things I already deleted
new items don't show up in search
rebuild the search index without downtime
keep Algolia in sync with my database
entries.summary: The jobs that copy changes from your database into a separate search engine. Every create, update and delete queues an index update, a full rebuild can run into a fresh index and swap over, and a check catches drift.
need_when: Search runs on a separate engine (Meilisearch, Typesense, Algolia, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) or a vector store.
skip_when: Search runs inside your main database (Postgres full-text), so it's always current.

ways.title: Queue an index job on every change
ways.how: After commit, enqueue upsert or delete jobs with the record id. The job reads the current row and updates the index.
ways.tradeoff: Near real time. Missed jobs leave drift unless you also reconcile.

ways.title: Library-managed sync
ways.how: Laravel Scout, Rails searchkick or meilisearch-rails, and similar packages hook into model saves.
ways.tradeoff: Little code. Bulk updates and raw SQL can skip the hooks.

ways.title: Full rebuild with an alias swap
ways.how: Build a new index from scratch, then point the alias or swap indexes in one step.
ways.tradeoff: Fixes all drift and schema changes with no downtime. Takes time and resources on big data.

entries.prompt:
Keep my [Meilisearch / Typesense / Algolia] index in sync with the database.

Requirements:
- After a transaction commits, enqueue index jobs for created, updated and deleted records (soft deletes and permission changes count as removals).
- The job loads the current row and upserts or deletes, so out-of-order jobs end up correct.
- Batch updates when many records change at once.
- A rebuild command: create a new index, fill it in batches, then swap it in with no search downtime.
- A nightly reconcile that compares ids and updated_at between database and index and fixes differences.
- Only index fields that are safe to show. Filter results by owner or tenant in every search query.
- Metrics: queue length, failed jobs and drift count.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A deleted record disappears from search within a minute.
2. Editing a title shows the new title in results.
3. Running the rebuild while searching causes no errors or empty results.
4. Breaking the worker for an hour, then fixing it, leaves no drift after reconcile.
5. A user never sees another tenant's records in results.
acceptance_checks: A deleted record disappears from search within a minute.
Editing a title shows the new title in results.
Running the rebuild while searching causes no errors or empty results.
Breaking the worker for an hour, then fixing it, leaves no drift after reconcile.
A user never sees another tenant's records in results.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Search shows deleted or private items and misses new ones, and users stop trusting it.

entries.name: Translations and localization (i18n)
needs: translate my app into Spanish
support multiple languages
show dates and prices the way each country expects
let users pick their language
entries.summary: Pulling every user-facing string out of the code into translation files, picking a language per user, and formatting dates, numbers, currencies and plurals with the locale's rules. Done early, it's cheap. Done late, it means touching every screen.
need_when: You have or want users who prefer another language.
You show dates, numbers or money to people in more than one country.
skip_when: One market, one language, no plans to change. Still use locale-aware date and number formatting.

ways.title: Your framework's i18n system
ways.how: Django gettext with .po files, Rails I18n, i18next or next-intl for React, vue-i18n, Flutter intl.
ways.tradeoff: Standard and free. You manage translation files and missing keys.

ways.title: A translation management platform
ways.how: Crowdin, Lokalise, Phrase, or open source Weblate or Tolgee sync files with your repo and give translators an editor.
ways.tradeoff: Smooth for many languages and translators. Another tool to run or pay for.

ways.title: Machine translation first, review after
ways.how: Translate new strings with an AI or translation API, then have a fluent speaker review key screens.
ways.tradeoff: Fast. Legal, billing and safety text needs human review.

entries.prompt:
Add translations to my app, starting with [Spanish].

Requirements:
- Use [framework i18n tool]. Move every user-facing string (pages, emails, errors, notifications) into translation keys.
- Whole sentences per key with placeholders, never sentences glued from pieces. Handle plurals with the library's plural rules.
- Language choice order: user setting, then the browser's Accept-Language, then [English]. Save the choice on the account and use it for emails too.
- Format dates, numbers and money with the locale (Intl API or framework helpers). Keep storing data in UTC and plain numbers.
- Set the html lang attribute. Make layouts survive 30 percent longer text.
- Add a check that fails CI on missing keys in any language file.
- Don't translate user-generated content.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Switching to Spanish changes pages, emails and error messages.
2. 1 item and 2 items use the right plural forms.
3. Dates show as 21/10/2026 for es-ES and 10/21/2026 for en-US.
4. Removing a key from the Spanish file fails CI.
5. No English strings remain on main screens in Spanish mode.
acceptance_checks: Switching to Spanish changes pages, emails and error messages.
1 item and 2 items use the right plural forms.
Dates show as 21/10/2026 for es-ES and 10/21/2026 for en-US.
Removing a key from the Spanish file fails CI.
No English strings remain on main screens in Spanish mode.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Half-translated screens, broken grammar from glued strings, and a painful rewrite when the first non-English customer arrives.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal has Django's i18n turned on with English and Spanish, the locale middleware, and a Spanish translation catalog in its locale folder.

entries.name: Calendar feeds and invites (ICS)
needs: let users see my app's events in Google Calendar
add an add-to-calendar button
a calendar subscription link that updates by itself
recurring events show at the wrong time after daylight saving
entries.summary: Publishing events in the iCalendar format so Google, Apple and Outlook calendars can show them. A one-off .ics file adds a single event. A private subscription URL lets the user's calendar refresh your events on its own schedule.
need_when: Your app has dates users care about: bookings, deadlines, schedules, classes, shifts.
skip_when: You need two-way sync (edits in Google flowing back). That needs the calendar APIs and OAuth, not a feed.

ways.title: A private ICS subscription URL
ways.how: A URL with a long random token returns text/calendar for that user. Calendar apps poll it.
ways.tradeoff: Works everywhere with no OAuth. Google can take hours to refresh, and the URL is the password.

ways.title: One-off .ics files and email invites
ways.how: A download or email attachment with one VEVENT for "add to calendar".
ways.tradeoff: Simple. Later changes don't reach the calendar unless you send an update.

ways.title: Calendar APIs
ways.how: Google Calendar API, Microsoft Graph or a unified API like Nylas or Cronofy write events into the user's calendar.
ways.tradeoff: Instant and two-way. OAuth setup, scopes review and token storage.

entries.prompt:
Add a private calendar subscription feed (ICS) for each user.

Requirements:
- URL: /calendar/feed/<token>.ics with a random token of at least 32 bytes stored on the user. No session needed. Unknown token returns 404.
- Settings page shows the link (plus a webcal:// version and Google and Apple instructions) and a "reset link" button that issues a new token.
- Return text/calendar; charset=utf-8. Each event has a stable UID, DTSTAMP, start and end, and SUMMARY. Escape commas, semicolons and newlines, and fold lines at 75 octets.
- Use the user's timezone with a VTIMEZONE block, or UTC times. All-day events use DATE values with an exclusive end date.
- Recurring items use RRULE inside a bounded window instead of expanding forever.
- Limit the feed to a window such as [1 year back, 2 years ahead]. Keep private notes out of the feed.
- Cache-Control: private. Validate output with an iCalendar validator in a test.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and Outlook all subscribe and show the events.
2. A weekly event stays at the same local time across the daylight saving change.
3. Resetting the link makes the old URL return 404.
4. Private notes never appear in the feed.
5. The feed passes an iCalendar validator.
acceptance_checks: Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and Outlook all subscribe and show the events.
A weekly event stays at the same local time across the daylight saving change.
Resetting the link makes the old URL return 404.
Private notes never appear in the feed.
The feed passes an iCalendar validator.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Events land an hour off twice a year, feeds leak private details to anyone with the link, or old links can't be shut off.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal offers a private calendar subscribe URL authenticated by a random token, with a reset button that issues a new one. The feed is served as text/calendar with Cache-Control private, includes VTIMEZONE blocks, uses RRULE for weekly activities inside a window of about 30 days back and a year ahead, and can be limited to one case or child.

links.title: Google Calendar: subscribe to a calendar by URL

entries.name: Location and distance search
needs: show places near the user
find all stores within 10 miles
turn an address into coordinates
sort results by distance
entries.summary: Storing latitude and longitude for things, turning addresses into coordinates (geocoding), and querying by distance with a spatial index. The user's own location comes from the browser with permission, or from a typed address or postcode.
need_when: "Near me" search, delivery zones, local listings, check-ins, or maps.
skip_when: City or region dropdowns are enough. Exact location is sensitive data, so don't collect it without a reason.

ways.title: PostGIS
ways.how: Add the PostGIS extension, store a geography(Point) column with a GiST index, and query with ST_DWithin and ST_Distance.
ways.tradeoff: Accurate and fast at scale. One extension to install (most hosted Postgres offers it).

ways.title: Your search engine's geo features
ways.how: Meilisearch, Typesense and Elasticsearch filter and sort by distance from a point.
ways.tradeoff: Great when search already lives there. Another index to keep in sync.

ways.title: Geocoding APIs
ways.how: Google Maps Platform, Mapbox, or open data via Nominatim (with its usage policy) or a self-hosted Photon or Pelias.
ways.tradeoff: Needed to turn addresses into points. Check terms: some forbid storing results or using them off their maps.

entries.prompt:
Add location search so users can find [things] near them.

Requirements:
- Store location as [PostGIS geography(Point, 4326)] with a GiST index.
- Geocode addresses when records are saved, in a background job, with [provider]. Save the coordinates and the provider's place id if the terms allow storing it.
- User location: a typed address or postcode first. Offer "use my location" with the browser Geolocation API only on click, and handle denial.
- Query by radius with ST_DWithin and sort by ST_Distance. Paginate.
- Show distances in miles or km by locale.
- Don't store the user's precise location unless needed. Round it in logs and analytics.
- Respect the geocoding provider's rate limits and caching rules.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A search 10 miles from a point returns only items inside that radius, nearest first.
2. The query uses the spatial index (EXPLAIN shows it).
3. Denying location permission falls back to typing a place.
4. Logs don't contain precise user coordinates.
5. Geocoding failures don't block saving a record.
acceptance_checks: A search 10 miles from a point returns only items inside that radius, nearest first.
The query uses the spatial index (EXPLAIN shows it).
Denying location permission falls back to typing a place.
Logs don't contain precise user coordinates.
Geocoding failures don't block saving a record.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Distance search scans every row and slows down, or you quietly collect precise location you didn't need.

entries.name: Live updates (WebSockets, SSE or polling)
needs: show new messages without refreshing
update the dashboard live
should I use websockets or polling
show who else is viewing the document
entries.summary: Getting changes to the browser as they happen. Polling asks every few seconds. Server-sent events stream one way from server to browser. WebSockets go both ways. Pick the simplest one that meets the delay users will notice.
need_when: Chat, collaborative editing, live dashboards, notifications, or anything where a stale screen causes mistakes.
skip_when: Updates every 30 seconds are fine. Polling is enough and much simpler.

ways.title: Polling
ways.how: Fetch an endpoint every few seconds, ideally with If-Modified-Since or a since cursor.
ways.tradeoff: Works everywhere, nothing new to run. Some delay and wasted requests.

ways.title: Server-sent events
ways.how: A long-lived HTTP response that streams events, with automatic reconnect in the browser's EventSource.
ways.tradeoff: Simple for server-to-browser updates. Proxies need buffering off and long timeouts.

ways.title: WebSockets, self-run
ways.how: Socket.IO, Django Channels, Phoenix Channels or Rails Action Cable, with Redis for fan-out across servers.
ways.tradeoff: Two-way and fast. Sticky connections, scaling and auth are your job.

ways.title: A hosted realtime service
ways.how: Pusher, Ably, Supabase Realtime, Liveblocks or PartyKit carry the connections. Your server publishes events.
ways.tradeoff: No connection servers to run. Per-connection or per-message pricing.

entries.prompt:
Add live updates for [feature] using [polling / SSE / WebSockets / hosted service].

Requirements:
- Explain the choice in two sentences based on how fresh the data must be and whether the browser sends data back.
- Authenticate the connection with the user's session or a short-lived token. Subscribe only to channels the user may see, checked on the server.
- Send small events (type, id, changed fields) and let the client fetch full data if needed.
- On reconnect, catch up from the last event id or timestamp so nothing is missed.
- Fall back to polling if the connection fails repeatedly.
- Configure the proxy for long-lived connections (timeouts, buffering off for SSE).
- With more than one server, fan out through [Redis pub/sub / the hosted service].

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A change made in one browser shows up in another within [2] seconds.
2. A user can't subscribe to another user's channel by changing its name.
3. Dropping the network for 30 seconds, then reconnecting, shows missed updates.
4. Two app servers both deliver events to their connected users.
5. Polling fallback works when WebSockets are blocked.
acceptance_checks: A change made in one browser shows up in another within [2] seconds.
A user can't subscribe to another user's channel by changing its name.
Dropping the network for 30 seconds, then reconnecting, shows missed updates.
Two app servers both deliver events to their connected users.
Polling fallback works when WebSockets are blocked.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Users see stale data and overwrite each other, or private updates go to the wrong browser.

entries.name: Internal admin panel
needs: I need a way to look up and fix customer records
build an admin dashboard for my app
stop editing the production database by hand
give support staff limited access
entries.summary: A private part of your app for you and your staff to find users, see their records, and fix common problems with buttons instead of raw SQL. Every action checks staff roles and lands in the audit log.
need_when: You or support have started running queries against production to help customers.
skip_when: Very early with a handful of users. A read-only database client with care may do for now.

ways.title: Your framework's admin
ways.how: Django admin, Rails ActiveAdmin or Avo, Laravel Filament or Nova, AdminJS for Node.
ways.tradeoff: Huge head start. Lock it down and keep it for staff only.

ways.title: An internal tools builder
ways.how: Retool, Appsmith, Budibase or ToolJet connect to your database or API and build screens by drag and drop.
ways.tradeoff: Fast for custom screens. Another service with access to production data.

ways.title: Custom admin pages in your app
ways.how: A /staff area built with your normal stack, behind staff roles.
ways.tradeoff: Fits your workflows exactly. Takes the longest.

entries.prompt:
Add an internal admin panel for staff using [tool].

Requirements:
- Separate URL path that's not guessable or linked publicly, staff-only, with 2FA required for staff accounts.
- Roles: [support] can view and do safe actions, [admin] can do everything. Check roles on the server for every action.
- Screens: find user by email or id, view their account, plan, recent activity and errors.
- Actions as buttons with confirmation: resend verification, extend trial, refund, disable account. No free-form SQL.
- Never show tokens or secrets. Hide private notes and other sensitive fields unless the task needs them.
- Log every view of a user record and every action with staff id, target and reason.
- Rate limit and alert on unusual admin activity, like bulk exports.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A normal user gets 404 on admin URLs.
2. Support role can't perform admin-only actions through the API.
3. Every action appears in the audit log with who, what and why.
4. Secrets and tokens never show in admin screens.
5. Common support tasks no longer need database access.
acceptance_checks: A normal user gets 404 on admin URLs.
Support role can't perform admin-only actions through the API.
Every action appears in the audit log with who, what and why.
Secrets and tokens never show in admin screens.
Common support tasks no longer need database access.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Staff fix things by hand in production SQL, mistakes go unrecorded, and one leaked staff login exposes every customer.

entries.name: Optimistic updates
needs: my app feels slow every time I click a button
the like button waits for the server before it changes
make my UI feel instant
entries.summary: Showing the result of an action on screen the moment the user clicks, then sending it to the server in the background. If the server says no, you put the old value back and tell the user. It makes small actions like likes, checkboxes and reordering feel instant.
need_when: Small, common actions that almost always succeed, like toggles, likes, renames and reordering.
Users notice a delay between clicking and seeing the change.
skip_when: Payments, deletes of important data, or anything where showing success and then taking it back would hurt or confuse people. Show a clear pending state there instead.

ways.title: Your data library's optimistic option
ways.how: TanStack Query's onMutate with rollback in onError, SWR's optimisticData, or the cache update in Apollo or RTK Query.
ways.tradeoff: Handles caching, rollback and refetching for you. Each action still needs its own update code.

ways.title: React useOptimistic
ways.how: Wrap the state you show in useOptimistic and set the new value before the server action runs.
ways.tradeoff: Built in and small. Works best with React server actions and forms.

ways.title: Write it by hand
ways.how: Save the old value, set the new one, send the request, and put the old value back if it fails.
ways.tradeoff: No library needed. Easy to miss the out-of-order and double-click cases.

entries.prompt:
Make these actions update the UI optimistically: [like button / todo checkbox / rename / reorder].

Requirements:
- Update the screen immediately when the user acts, then send the request in the background.
- Keep the previous value. If the request fails or times out, restore it and show a short error the user can see.
- After the request settles, refetch or replace with the server's version so the screen matches the database.
- If the user clicks again before the first request finishes, the last click wins and the screen never flickers between old states.
- Do not use optimistic updates for [payments / deletes / anything listed here]. Show a pending state there instead.
- Use [TanStack Query / SWR / useOptimistic / the existing data layer] and follow its documented rollback pattern.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Clicking like (or done) updates the screen right away, before the server answers.
2. With the network throttled to Slow 3G in dev tools, the change still shows instantly.
3. When the server returns an error, the screen goes back to the old value and shows a message.
4. Clicking the same button five times fast ends with the right final state after a refresh.
acceptance_checks: Clicking like (or done) updates the screen right away, before the server answers.
With the network throttled to Slow 3G in dev tools, the change still shows instantly.
When the server returns an error, the screen goes back to the old value and shows a message.
Clicking the same button five times fast ends with the right final state after a refresh.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Every click waits on a round trip, so the app feels sluggish even when the server is fine. Done badly, you get the opposite problem: changes that look saved but quietly were not.

entries.name: Autosave and drafts
needs: users lose what they typed when the page refreshes
save drafts automatically while people type
warn before leaving with unsaved changes
entries.summary: Saving what a user is writing every few seconds without them pressing Save, usually as a draft that only becomes the real record when they finish. A refresh, crash or dead battery then costs them a few seconds of typing, not the whole thing.
need_when: Long forms, editors, or anything people type into for more than a minute.
Users write on phones, where tabs get killed in the background.
skip_when: Short forms of a few fields. A warning before leaving the page is enough.

ways.title: Save to the browser
ways.how: Write the form to localStorage on a short debounce and restore it on load. Clear it after a real save.
ways.tradeoff: No server changes and works offline. Lost if they switch devices or clear the browser.

ways.title: Server-side draft
ways.how: Post the content on a debounce to a draft endpoint that updates one draft row per user and record, then promote it on Save.
ways.tradeoff: Survives any device or crash. You must keep drafts out of every list, count and export.

ways.title: An editor with built-in autosave
ways.how: Rich text or form libraries that ship an autosave plugin, or collaborative editors that save every change.
ways.tradeoff: Least code. Ties you to that editor's storage model.

entries.prompt:
Add autosave with drafts to [form / editor].

Requirements:
- Save the content [2] seconds after the user stops typing, and when the field loses focus or the page is hidden.
- Store it as a draft, one draft per user per [record], updated in place instead of a new row each time.
- Keep drafts out of normal lists, search, exports, notifications and usage limits until the user presses Save.
- Show a small status near the form: Saving, Saved, or a clear error if it failed.
- If the record changed somewhere else since it was loaded, stop autosaving and show a conflict message instead of overwriting.
- Warn with beforeunload only when there are changes that have not been saved yet.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Typing in the form, waiting 3 seconds and refreshing brings the text back.
2. The save status changes from Saving to Saved, and to an error when the network is off.
3. Autosaving 20 times leaves one draft, not 20 records.
4. Drafts don't show in lists, search, exports or usage counts until the user presses Save.
5. Editing the same record in two tabs shows a conflict message instead of silently overwriting.
acceptance_checks: Typing in the form, waiting 3 seconds and refreshing brings the text back.
The save status changes from Saving to Saved, and to an error when the network is off.
Autosaving 20 times leaves one draft, not 20 records.
Drafts don't show in lists, search, exports or usage counts until the user presses Save.
Editing the same record in two tabs shows a conflict message instead of silently overwriting.
entries.if_you_skip_it: People lose long pieces of writing to a refresh or a dropped connection, and they rarely come back after that. Done carelessly, half-finished drafts show up as real records.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: The Custody Journal entry form autosaves about 2 seconds after typing stops. Each user gets one draft per custody case, drafts are hidden from every list and report and don't count against the free plan, and the draft becomes a real entry only when the user presses Save. Autosave stops with a warning if the entry changed elsewhere, and it never rewrites an entry that has already been sealed.

entries.name: Cookie consent and privacy-friendly analytics
needs: do I need a cookie banner
load Google Analytics only after people agree
track visits without cookies
entries.summary: Asking before you set non-essential cookies or load trackers, where the law requires it, and not loading them until people agree. Many apps avoid most of the problem by using cookieless, privacy-focused analytics and keeping ad pixels off logged-in pages.
need_when: You have visitors in the UK or EU and use analytics, ad pixels or other non-essential cookies.
skip_when: You only set cookies strictly needed for the service, like login and CSRF. Check the rules for where your users are.

ways.title: Cookieless analytics
ways.how: Umami, Plausible or GoatCounter (self-hosted or their cloud) count visits without tracking cookies.
ways.tradeoff: Often no banner needed for analytics, but check the rules where your users are. Less detail than ad-tech tools.

ways.title: A small consent banner you build
ways.how: Store the choice in a first-party cookie and only inject third-party scripts after 'Accept'. Make 'Reject' as easy as 'Accept'.
ways.tradeoff: Light and fully controlled. You maintain the list of what each choice loads.

ways.title: A consent management platform
ways.how: A hosted consent tool, or Google's consent mode alongside it if you use Google tags.
ways.tradeoff: Handles many vendors and regions. Heavier pages and another vendor.

entries.prompt:
Set up consent-aware analytics for this app.

Requirements:
- List every cookie and third-party script the app loads, and mark each as strictly necessary or not.
- Load nothing non-essential (analytics, ad pixels, chat widgets) until the visitor accepts. Reject must be one click and as visible as Accept.
- Store the choice in a first-party cookie, and add a link in the footer to change it later.
- Keep third-party trackers off logged-in pages and pages with personal data entirely.
- If possible, switch analytics to a cookieless tool so the banner covers less.
- Update the privacy policy to match what's actually loaded.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. With no choice made, the network tab shows no requests to analytics or ad domains.
2. After Reject, still none.
3. After Accept, the chosen scripts load.
4. Logged-in pages never load ad pixels, whatever the choice.
acceptance_checks: With no choice made, the network tab shows no requests to analytics or ad domains.
After Reject, still none.
After Accept, the chosen scripts load.
Logged-in pages never load ad pixels, whatever the choice.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Complaints and fines under privacy laws, and personal data from inside your app leaking to ad networks.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal loads third-party analytics only for signed-out visitors, only on the home, start and pricing pages, and only after the cj_analytics_consent_v1 cookie is set to granted.

entries.name: Data export and account deletion
needs: let users delete their account and everything in it
let users download all their data
Apple requires in-app account deletion
entries.summary: Self-serve tools for users to download their data in a usable format and to delete their account. Deleting means removing their records and files, cancelling their billing, and telling them what's kept and why, like backups that expire or legal records.
need_when: You have users in places with privacy laws (UK, EU, California and others).
Your iOS app lets people create accounts: Apple requires account deletion inside the app.
skip_when: Rarely. Even small apps get these requests, and doing them by hand is error-prone.

ways.title: Self-serve export as a background job
ways.how: A job builds a zip with JSON or CSV (and files), stores it privately, and emails a signed link that expires.
ways.tradeoff: Handles big accounts without timeouts. You maintain it as models change.

ways.title: Self-serve deletion with confirmation
ways.how: Re-authenticate, type a word to confirm, cancel billing first, then delete records and schedule file cleanup after the transaction commits.
ways.tradeoff: No support tickets. Make sure nothing is left in other systems, like email lists or analytics.

ways.title: A documented manual process
ways.how: A request form and a checklist covering every system that holds user data.
ways.tradeoff: Fine at low volume. Slow, and easy to forget a system.

entries.prompt:
Add self-serve data export and account deletion.

Requirements:
- Export: a background job builds a zip of all the user's data as JSON and CSV, plus their uploaded files. It's stored privately and delivered by an expiring signed link. Exclude other users' private data and internal fields.
- Deletion: require the user to re-authenticate and type DELETE. Cancel any subscription first, and stop if billing can't be confirmed closed.
- Delete the user's records in one transaction. Schedule file deletion to run after the transaction commits.
- Remove them from email lists, analytics and any other service that holds their data. List each one.
- Tell the user what is kept and for how long (backups, invoices, legal records).
- On iOS, make deletion reachable from inside the app.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The export opens and contains every type of record the user created.
2. After deletion, the user can't log in and their records and files are gone.
3. Their subscription is cancelled in the payment provider.
4. They're removed from the email list.
5. If billing can't be confirmed closed, nothing is deleted and the user sees why.
acceptance_checks: The export opens and contains every type of record the user created.
After deletion, the user can't log in and their records and files are gone.
Their subscription is cancelled in the payment provider.
They're removed from the email list.
If billing can't be confirmed closed, nothing is deleted and the user sees why.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Privacy complaints, app store rejection, and 'deleted' users who keep getting billed or emailed.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal exports a full zip with JSON, CSV, a calendar file, vCard contacts and an expenses spreadsheet, plus a separate documents zip. To delete an account, the user types DELETE, and the app refuses to go on unless it can confirm Stripe billing is closed. It then records file cleanup tasks and deletes the user in one transaction, with cleanup running after commit, and tells the user that encrypted backups and limited legal records may remain until their retention ends.

entries.name: Data retention and cleanup
needs: how long should I keep user data
delete old logs automatically
my database keeps growing with stuff nobody needs
a customer asks how long we keep their data
entries.summary: A written list of what data you keep, for how long and why, plus scheduled jobs that delete or anonymize it when time is up. It covers logs, backups, temporary files, expired tokens and closed accounts.
need_when: You store personal data, logs or files. Privacy laws such as GDPR expect you not to keep data longer than needed.
Tables like sessions, events and logs grow forever.
skip_when: Never. Even a short policy with two cleanup jobs beats none.

ways.title: Scheduled delete jobs
ways.how: A daily job per data type deletes rows older than the limit, in small batches.
ways.tradeoff: Simple and visible. Each new table needs its own rule.

ways.title: Built-in expiry
ways.how: Redis key TTLs, object storage lifecycle rules (S3, R2), log platform retention settings, and Postgres partition dropping for big time-series tables.
ways.tradeoff: Hands-off once set. Easy to forget backups and copies.

ways.title: Anonymize instead of delete
ways.how: Remove or hash personal fields but keep aggregate rows for reporting.
ways.tradeoff: Keeps stats. Make sure it can't be re-identified.

entries.prompt:
Write and apply a data retention policy for my app.

Requirements:
- List every place data is stored: tables, file storage, logs, backups, analytics, error tracking, email provider, AI provider.
- For each: what's kept, why, how long ([30 days / 1 year / until account deletion]), and delete or anonymize.
- Add a scheduled job per rule that deletes in batches with a row limit per run and logs counts.
- Set TTLs or lifecycle rules where the platform supports them (Redis, object storage, logs).
- Make sure backups roll off within a stated window, and note it in the privacy policy.
- When an account is deleted, cover every store in the list.
- Produce the policy as a short page I can link from the privacy policy.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Rows older than each limit are gone after the job runs.
2. Each cleanup job logs how many rows it removed.
3. Bucket lifecycle rules show the stated expiry.
4. The policy page matches what the jobs actually do.
5. A deleted test account leaves nothing in the listed stores beyond backups, which roll off on schedule.
acceptance_checks: Rows older than each limit are gone after the job runs.
Each cleanup job logs how many rows it removed.
Bucket lifecycle rules show the stated expiry.
The policy page matches what the jobs actually do.
A deleted test account leaves nothing in the listed stores beyond backups, which roll off on schedule.
entries.if_you_skip_it: You keep years of personal data you don't need, which raises breach damage, storage cost and legal risk.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal's scheduler runs daily prune jobs, for example deleting operations heartbeat rows older than 30 days and expired plugin credentials after a 7-day retention window.

entries.name: Product analytics events
needs: I don't know where users drop off
track signups and conversions in my app
which features do people actually use
entries.summary: Sending a small named event when a user does something that matters, like signing up, finishing setup or upgrading, so you can count each step and see where people stop. Page views tell you traffic. Events tell you whether the product is working.
need_when: You want to know how many visitors sign up, activate and pay.
You are deciding what to build next and want usage, not guesses.
skip_when: You have a handful of users you can just talk to. A few queries on your own database may answer the question.

ways.title: Privacy-friendly page analytics with custom events
ways.how: Umami or Plausible, with a few custom events on the buttons and forms that matter.
ways.tradeoff: Light, cookieless and easy. Basic funnels only.

ways.title: A product analytics tool
ways.how: PostHog or Mixpanel, with server-side events for signups and payments and a user id that is not an email.
ways.tradeoff: Real funnels, retention and cohorts. More setup and more privacy work.

ways.title: Your own events table
ways.how: Write a row per important event to your database and query it.
ways.tradeoff: You own the data and it never leaves. You build the charts yourself.

entries.prompt:
Add product analytics events for this funnel: [landing view, signup, first key action, upgrade, paid].

Requirements:
- Write down an event list first: snake_case names, when each fires, and its properties. Keep it under [10] events.
- Send signup and payment events from the server, after the database write succeeds, so ad blockers and refreshes don't change the counts.
- Use an id that is not personal, like a hash of the user id. Never send emails, names, or text the user typed.
- Respect the existing consent setting. If consent is declined, send nothing to third parties.
- Make each event fire once per real action, not once per page render or retry.
- Use [Umami / Plausible / PostHog / an events table] and put the tracking calls in one small helper module.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Signing up in staging creates exactly one sign_up event with the agreed properties.
2. A funnel from landing page view to paid shows a count for every step.
3. No event payload contains an email, name or free text the user typed.
4. With analytics consent declined, the network tab shows no requests to the analytics provider.
acceptance_checks: Signing up in staging creates exactly one sign_up event with the agreed properties.
A funnel from landing page view to paid shows a count for every step.
No event payload contains an email, name or free text the user typed.
With analytics consent declined, the network tab shows no requests to the analytics provider.
entries.if_you_skip_it: You guess where users get stuck, ship features nobody uses, and can't tell whether a change helped. Tracked carelessly, you leak personal data into a third party.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal saves a fixed list of funnel events, from signup intent through subscription started, to its own database. It sends events to PostHog only for signed-out visitors on the home, start and pricing pages after they accept analytics, and uses a hashed id instead of the account id or email.
